input:
The goal is the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min, computed from a measured rate constant. The half-life is 57.8 min and the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.49.

For a first-order reaction, the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k. The fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). The half-life is the time at which the fraction remaining is one half, read directly from the decay relation. Both relations rest on the same statement: the rate of reaction at any instant is proportional to the concentration still present, so equal fractions disappear in equal times and the decay has no memory of how long it has already run.

The measured rate constant is k = 0.012 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. The sampling interval is short against the half-life, so the decay curve is fixed by many points rather than by the endpoints alone.

Substitution in the half-life relation gives t1/2 = ln(2) / 0.012 = 57.8 min. Substitution in the decay relation at t = 60 min gives exp(-0.012 x 60) = exp(-0.72) = 0.49. The two results agree in the way they must: 60 min stands just past the half-life of 57.8 min, so the fraction remaining stands just below one half.

The relations hold for a first-order reaction only. A reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and its half-life is not fixed by the rate constant alone in the same way.
